entries.content: A blood glucose test measures the amount of glucose (sugar) in the blood and is used to screen for and monitor diabetes and prediabetes. A fasting test is usually done after having nothing to eat or drink except water for at least 8 hours. For fasting glucose, MedlinePlus lists 99 mg/dL or lower as normal, 100 to 125 mg/dL as prediabetes and 126 mg/dL or higher as diabetes, and a diagnosis normally needs a repeat test to confirm it. The interval printed by the patient's own laboratory still applies to the report.

entries.content: Some blood tests, most often glucose tests and some cholesterol or triglyceride tests, require fasting so that a recent meal does not change the result. Fasting usually means no food or drink other than water for 8 to 12 hours before the sample is taken, so these tests are often scheduled in the morning. Drinking water is normally allowed. Many other blood tests need no fasting, so the instructions of the ordering clinician or laboratory decide; anyone who ate or drank by mistake should tell the staff, because the test may need to be rescheduled.

entries.content: Hemoglobin is the iron-containing protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body. The test is usually part of a complete blood count and is mainly used to check for anemia. A low level may be linked to anemia from causes such as iron deficiency, blood loss, vitamin deficiencies or inherited hemoglobin disorders such as thalassemia, while a high level can occur with dehydration, smoking, living at high altitude or some lung, heart or bone-marrow conditions. Normal ranges differ by age, sex and laboratory.

entries.content: A white blood count measures the number of white blood cells, which help the body fight infections and other diseases, and is part of a complete blood count. A differential count shows the main types: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. A high count can occur with infection, inflammation, stress, some medicines or, less commonly, blood disorders; a low count can occur with some viral infections, autoimmune conditions, bone-marrow problems or certain medical treatments. A single result is interpreted with symptoms and other tests.

A low count (thrombocytopenia) can increase the risk of bruising or bleeding and may be linked to certain infections, medicines, autoimmune conditions, bone-marrow problems or an enlarged spleen. A high count (thrombocytosis) can occur with inflammation, infection, iron deficiency or bone-marrow disorders. Further tests may be needed to find the cause of an abnormal count.

entries.content: Red blood cell indices are part of a complete blood count and describe the size and hemoglobin content of red cells: MCV is the average cell size, MCH the average amount of hemoglobin per cell, MCHC the hemoglobin concentration in the cells and RDW the variation in size. They help classify anemia: small, pale cells (low MCV and MCH) are seen with iron deficiency and thalassemia, while large cells (high MCV) can be seen with vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. The indices guide further testing rather than giving a diagnosis on their own.

entries.content: Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood that the body uses for energy; high levels can raise the risk of heart disease, and very high levels can also cause pancreatitis. The test is usually part of a lipid panel, and fasting may be requested because a recent meal raises triglycerides. For adults, MedlinePlus describes less than 150 mg/dL as normal, 150 to 199 mg/dL as borderline high, 200 to 499 mg/dL as high and 500 mg/dL or more as very high. The result is interpreted with the rest of the lipid profile and personal risk factors.

entries.content: HDL (high-density lipoprotein) is called "good" cholesterol because it carries cholesterol from other parts of the body back to the liver, which removes it from the body. Higher HDL levels are generally linked to a lower risk of heart disease, and a low HDL is one of the risk factors a clinician considers. MedlinePlus lists a healthy HDL level for adults as 40 mg/dL or higher for men and 50 mg/dL or higher for women. HDL is measured in a lipid panel and read together with LDL, triglycerides and other risk factors.

LDL is reported in a lipid panel, either calculated from the other values or measured directly. MedlinePlus gives a healthy LDL level for adults as less than 100 mg/dL. Because the right goal depends on a person's overall cardiovascular risk, the result is discussed with a clinician together with other risk factors.

entries.content: A BUN test measures urea nitrogen, a waste product made when the liver breaks down protein and removed from the blood by the kidneys. It is often ordered with creatinine, for example in a basic metabolic panel, to check kidney function. A high BUN can occur with kidney disease, dehydration, a high-protein diet, heart failure, bleeding in the digestive tract or some medicines; a low BUN is less common and may be seen with liver disease or malnutrition. A BUN-to-creatinine ratio is sometimes reported to help interpretation.

entries.content: A urinalysis checks the appearance, concentration and content of urine with a visual exam, a dipstick test (for example for protein, glucose, ketones, blood, nitrite and white cells) and sometimes a microscope exam for cells, crystals and casts. It is used in routine check-ups and to look for urinary tract infections, kidney disease, diabetes and other conditions. A clean-catch midstream sample is usually collected. Abnormal findings often need repeat or follow-up tests, because diet, medicines, exercise, menstruation or contamination can affect the result.

entries.content: ALT (alanine transaminase, also called SGPT) is an enzyme found mostly in the liver; when liver cells are damaged, ALT is released into the bloodstream. The test, usually part of a liver panel, is used to check for liver damage. A high ALT can be caused by conditions such as viral hepatitis, fatty liver, alcohol-related liver disease, some medicines or other liver problems. The size of the rise does not by itself identify the cause, so ALT is interpreted together with AST, other liver tests and clinical information.

The test is used to help detect liver disease, especially conditions affecting the bile ducts, and bone disorders. High levels can occur with liver or bile duct problems or with bone conditions; children and teenagers normally have higher levels because their bones are growing, and levels also rise in pregnancy. Other tests, such as GGT, can help show whether a high ALP comes from the liver or from bone.

A low level may be related to liver disease, kidney disease in which albumin is lost in urine, malnutrition, inflammation or other conditions; a high level is uncommon and is usually linked to dehydration. Results are interpreted with other liver and kidney tests.

A bilirubin test measures total bilirubin and sometimes direct (conjugated) and indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin. High levels can cause jaundice (yellow skin and eyes) and may be related to liver disease, blocked bile ducts or increased breakdown of red blood cells. Gilbert syndrome, a common inherited condition, can cause mildly raised bilirubin that is usually harmless.

entries.content: NIDDK explains that early kidney disease usually has no symptoms, so blood and urine tests are the only way to know how the kidneys are working. A creatinine blood test is used to estimate the glomerular filtration rate (eGFR): an eGFR of 60 or more is in the normal range, below 60 may mean kidney disease, and 15 or less may mean kidney failure. A urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR) below 30 mg/g is normal, while 30 mg/g or more may be a sign of kidney disease. Because results can change for temporary reasons, abnormal tests are repeated over about 3 months to confirm kidney disease.
